# `aitbc wallet restore`

Restore a wallet from a backup file with an optional force override. Encryption state is preserved verbatim: an already-encrypted backup is written back as-is (still under its original password). A plaintext backup stays plaintext unless ``--password-file`` or ``--password-stdin`` is given — then the restored key is encrypted under it (PBKDF2 + Fernet, atomic 0600 write). There is deliberately no ``--password`` argv option: a password flag on an already-encrypted backup is an explicit error, never a silent ignore; nothing is written in that case.

## Usage

```bash
aitbc wallet restore [OPTIONS]
```

## Options

| Option | Type | Default | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--backup-path` | text | — | yes | Path to the backup file. |
| `--name` | text | — | yes | Wallet name. |
| `--force` | flag | `false` | no | Override existing wallet |
| `--password-file` | file | — | no | Path to a file containing only the wallet password (mode 0600, owned by you) — encrypts a plaintext backup on restore |
| `--password-stdin` | flag | `false` | no | Read the wallet password from one line of standard input — encrypts a plaintext backup on restore |

## Examples

```bash
aitbc wallet restore --backup-path <backup_path> --name <name>
```
